title: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Modify Cloud Compute Configurations
shortTitle: Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Modify Cloud Compute...
summary: This sub-technique targets the settings that acting as guard rails around cloud compute: service quotas, subscription associations, tenant-wide policies, and the regional or size constraints that determine what a subscription is allowed to deploy. Rather than touching a running machine, the adversary changes what the platform will permit, which can be far quieter. A successful quota increase request looks like ordinary capacity planning, yet it unlocks room for large numbers of instances used for resource hijacking, so the victim sees only normal consumption that stays inside a ceiling nobody was watching. Similarly, relaxing a policy that restricts virtual machine sizes, or enabling a region the organisation does not use, widens the deployment surface and can place workloads outside the coverage of regional logging and controls. Detection is configuration-focused: audit events for quota increase requests, policy definition edits, subscription or management group changes, and region enablement, correlated with a subsequent rise in provisioning activity that is not explained by a change request. Baselining which identities and roles normally alter policy or request quota, and reviewing the resulting resource growth, is what separates routine capacity management from abuse.

beginner.definition: Cloud providers put limits on an account, such as how many machines you may run or how large they can be. Administrators can ask for higher limits or change the rules. This technique means an attacker changes those limits. They are not adding a machine yet, they are changing what is allowed.
beginner.whyItMatters: A raised limit lets an attacker run many machines without tripping the usual alarms. The request looks like normal planning work, so it rarely gets questioned. Changing where resources may run can also put them outside your watched regions. This makes the abuse harder to see and harder to stop. It also wastes money if the machines are used for mining or spam.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access to an account that can change cloud settings.
They request a higher quota, which raises the maximum allowed usage.
They may edit a policy that limits machine sizes or allowed services.
They may enable a region your team does not use or monitor.
With the new room, they deploy machines that would previously be blocked.
Because each machine stays within the raised limit, no cap alarm fires.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel where the manager has told the kitchen to serve at most fifty guests. Someone edits that instruction sheet to five hundred. The kitchen follows the sheet exactly, and each single guest still looks ordinary. Nobody notices until the bills arrive.
takeaways: Treat quota increases and policy edits as security-relevant changes.
Review new limits against the reason given for the request.
Watch for use of regions or machine sizes your team never uses.

objectives: Name the cloud settings that control what compute can be deployed.
Explain why a quota or policy change is quieter than creating resources.
Describe how policy and region changes widen the attack surface.
Identify audit events for quota requests and policy modifications.
Recommend approval and review steps for configuration changes.
